name: AI Documentation Tools at Trial Sites
blurb: Reducing the documentation load on site staff.
title: AI Documentation Tools at Trial Sites
answer: Much trial work at sites is documentation, and AI scribes and assistants built for clinical care are being applied to it. One vendor reported that at a large health system its AI documentation assistant cut time spent on clinical notes by 72 percent, the kind of saving trial sites are now seeking.

reading.body:
AI documentation tools built for clinical care are being applied to trial site paperwork, with one vendor reporting a 72 percent cut in note-writing time at a large health system.

The pattern is a transfer of a tool from one setting to another. Documentation burden is a known problem in clinical care, and the same burden sits on trial site staff. A vendor that has already measured a reduction in note time at a health system offers a number that trial sites can use to justify trying the same class of tool.

The constraint is that an AI generated source document at a site still needs investigator review before it becomes trial data. The saving is in drafting, not in the review step, and the review step is what makes the output usable. A 72 percent reduction in time spent writing notes does not mean a 72 percent reduction in the work of producing a trial record.

The data covers one vendor and one health system. It does not say whether the same reduction holds at trial sites, whether the tool meets the requirements that trial documentation carries, or how review time changes when drafts arrive faster. Those are the questions a site would need answered before treating the number as its own.

explainer:
Trial sites carry a heavy documentation load: source records of each visit, case report form entries, adverse event reports, and correspondence with sponsors and ethics committees. Much of it duplicates clinical documentation already written for patient care, and it takes time from staff who are often stretched.

AI documentation assistants, first built for clinicians, draft notes from recorded conversations and pull information into structured forms. Applied carefully at trial sites, they can cut time spent on paperwork. Two rules apply. The investigator remains responsible for the accuracy of source documents, so every AI generated record must be reviewed and confirmed. And recording participants requires their consent and must follow the trial's approved procedures and privacy rules.
